Madrid on foot

The must-sees

  • Cibeles Fountain

    Landmark · 1782

    It was designed by Ventura Rodríguez in the reign of Charles III. Real Madrid fans gather here to celebrate their trophies.

    Look for: Behind the fountain rises the white Palace of Communications, built as the main post office and now Madrid’s city hall.

  • Gran Vía

    Shopping

    Work on the street began in 1910, cutting through a tangle of old lanes. Built in stages over decades, it shows how Madrid absorbed Paris, Chicago and New York styles.

    Look for: Find the Telefónica Building, finished in 1929: Madrid’s first skyscraper.

  • Metropolis Building

    Building · 1911

    It was finished in 1911 for the insurance company La Unión y el Fénix, whose phoenix first topped the dome. The Victory statue replaced it when the building changed owners in the 1970s.

    Look for: Look up at the dark slate dome trimmed in gold, and the bronze Victory spreading her wings above it.

  • Plaza Mayor

    Square · 1619

    Juan Gómez de Mora finished it in 1619 for Philip III. It has hosted bullfights, coronations and trials of the Inquisition, and was rebuilt several times after fires.

    Look for: The Casa de la Panadería, once the bakers’ guild house, on the north side has a facade painted with mythological figures in 1992.

  • Prado Museum

    Museum · 1819

    Juan de Villanueva designed it for Charles III as a natural history cabinet, but it opened in 1819 as a royal picture gallery. Velázquez’s Las Meninas hangs inside.

    Look for: Velázquez stands in bronze before the main west entrance; Murillo’s statue faces the Botanical Garden at the south end.

  • Puerta de Alcalá

    Landmark · 1778

    Francesco Sabatini built it for Charles III and it was finished in 1778. It once marked the road out of the city towards Alcalá de Henares.

    Look for: Walk around it: the two faces differ. The story goes that Charles III liked both of Sabatini’s designs and could not choose.

  • Puerta del Sol

    Square

    A plaque on the pavement marks Kilometre Zero, the point from which Spain’s national roads are measured. On New Year’s Eve crowds eat twelve grapes to the twelve strokes of the clock.

    Look for: Find the bronze bear reaching up into a strawberry tree, the emblem of Madrid.

  • Reina Sofía Museum

    Museum

    The building was the city’s general hospital in the 18th century. Picasso’s Guernica, painted after the 1937 bombing of the Basque town, has hung here since 1992.

    Look for: Behind the old hospital, Jean Nouvel’s extension sits under a vast red-tinted roof.

  • Retiro Park

    Park

    It began as the garden of a 17th-century royal palace built for Philip IV. It opened to the public in 1868, and in 2021 it became part of a UNESCO World Heritage site with the Paseo del Prado.

    Look for: Find the Crystal Palace, a glass-and-iron pavilion beside a small lake, built in 1887 for an exhibition on the Philippines.

  • Royal Palace

    Palace

    It replaced the old Moorish-era Alcázar, which burned on Christmas Eve 1734. It is still the king’s official residence, though the royal family lives at the Zarzuela Palace outside the centre.

    Look for: On the Plaza de Oriente side, find the row of stone kings: they were carved to stand along the palace roofline.

  • Santiago Bernabéu Stadium

    Venue · 1947

    It opened in 1947 and was later named after Santiago Bernabéu, the club president who built it. A recent rebuilding added a retractable roof and the metal facade.

  • Temple of Debod

    Landmark

    Egypt gave it to Spain in thanks for help saving Nubian monuments from the waters of the Aswan High Dam. It was rebuilt here stone by stone and opened in 1972, and its terrace is a favourite place to watch the sunset.

    Look for: Two stone gateways stand in the pool in front of the temple: they marked the processional way to it in Nubia.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Madrid and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Madrid passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
